content: 1. Individuals who are not receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART) derive greater benefit from isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) compared to those who are tuberculin skin test (TST) negative. Therefore, TST is recommended where feasible, such as with the use of diagnostic tools like Xpert MTB/RIF. 2. Patients with suspected or confirmed tuberculosis (TB) should be separated from others to prevent transmission. Cough etiquette and respiratory hygiene must be enforced, potentially through community-based approaches. These administrative measures are strongly recommended, although the evidence supporting them is of low quality. 3. Healthcare workers and caregivers should be informed and encouraged to undergo TB diagnostic testing if they exhibit TB symptoms. They should also be tested for HIV and provided with counseling. 4. HIV-positive healthcare workers should receive a comprehensive care package, including ART and IPT. If necessary, they should be relocated to areas with lower TB transmission risk. These recommendations are strongly advised in high HIV prevalence settings and conditionally recommended in low prevalence settings, supported by high-quality evidence. 5. Healthcare workers caring for patients with infectious TB (suspected or confirmed) should be provided with particulate respirator masks that meet or exceed N95 standards (CDC/NIOSH) or FFP2 standards (CE-certified). This is a strong recommendation, though based on low-quality evidence. 6. Environmental measures, such as natural or mechanical ventilation, are strongly recommended to reduce TB transmission, despite low-quality evidence. Upper-room ultraviolet germicidal irradiation is conditionally recommended, also based on low-quality evidence. 7. Healthcare facilities and congregate settings pose a high risk for TB transmission, including multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), particularly for people living with HIV and healthcare workers. National TB and HIV programs should provide managerial direction for implementing TB infection control measures. 8. Each healthcare facility should have a TB infection control plan that includes administrative, environmental, and personal protection measures. These plans should also address measures to protect healthcare workers and caregivers from TB transmission. 9. Periodic evaluation of infection control practices is essential to ensure appropriate measures are in place. Facility-level assessments of TB infection control should be integrated into routine supervisory activities in all healthcare facilities providing care for people living with HIV. 10. A standardized checklist for periodic evaluation of infection control practices can be used to measure progress over time. An example of such a checklist, adaptable to local contexts, is available in Annex 16. 11. To reduce TB transmission to families and communities, patients and their family members should be provided with key information. This includes advice on cough etiquette, sleeping alone, avoiding congregate settings and public transport while smear-positive, and spending as much time as possible outdoors when feasible. 12. MDR-TB is defined as TB that is resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampicin. Patients with both HIV and MDR-TB face complex clinical management, limited treatment options, and poorer outcomes. Systematic reviews have shown a concerning association between HIV and primary MDR-TB. 13. Outbreaks of MDR-TB among people with HIV have been documented in hospitals and other settings, particularly in Eastern Europe and Southern Africa, where HIV prevalence is high. Contributing factors include unrecognized drug resistance, inadequate isolation procedures, and insufficient treatment. 14. Extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) is a form of TB resistant to any fluoroquinolone and at least one of three second-line injectable drugs (capreomycin, kanamycin, or amikacin), in addition to multidrug resistance. The association between HIV and XDR-TB remains unclear, but rapid and deadly spread among people living with HIV has been observed. 15. Nosocomial outbreaks of XDR-TB involving people with HIV highlight the need for intensified infection control efforts in healthcare settings. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is recommended for all patients with HIV and drug-resistant TB requiring second-line anti-TB drugs, regardless of CD4 cell count. ART should be initiated as early as possible, within the first eight weeks of starting anti-TB treatment. 16. Xpert MTB/RIF is recommended as the initial diagnostic test for adults and children suspected of having HIV-associated TB due to the high mortality associated with unrecognized drug-resistant TB in people with HIV. Those with MDR-TB or rifampicin resistance should undergo further testing for second-line anti-TB drug resistance. 17. People with HIV who have MDR/XDR-TB should start ART as soon as possible, within eight weeks of initiating TB treatment. WHO has issued recommendations on the use of novel anti-TB drugs like delamanid and bedaquiline, which may also be used in people living with HIV. However, bedaquiline should be used cautiously in individuals over 65 years, those with diabetes, HIV, hepatic or severe renal impairment, or those who use alcohol or other substances, as data on efficacy and safety in these conditions are limited. 18. People with HIV are at higher risk of adverse drug reactions to both TB and non-TB medications, and this risk increases with the degree of immunosuppression. The complexity of antiretroviral (ARV) regimens and second-line TB treatment requires rigorous clinical monitoring due to their toxicity profiles and potential interactions. 19. Appropriate TB infection control measures in facilities caring for people with HIV, along with efforts to optimize adherence and completion of TB treatment, are critical to reducing the incidence of MDR-TB. Strengthening HIV prevention, improving collaboration between HIV and TB programs, and focusing on high-risk groups (e.g., people who inject drugs, those in prisons or congregate settings) can also help minimize MDR-TB. 20. Cryptococcal meningitis is a common opportunistic infection and a leading cause of death in people with HIV, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia. Delayed presentation, poor availability, and high cost of treatment contribute to the high mortality rate. WHO published rapid advice in 2011 on the diagnosis, prevention, and management of cryptococcal disease in HIV-infected individuals. 21. Early diagnosis and treatment with amphotericin B-based regimens are recommended as part of a minimum package of toxicity prevention, monitoring, and management. Prompt management of raised intracranial pressure and systematic evaluation of clinically deteriorating patients are also advised. 22. ART initiation in HIV-infected patients with cryptococcal meningitis should be deferred until there is evidence of a sustained clinical response to antifungal therapy. ART should begin after four weeks of induction and consolidation treatment with amphotericin B-containing regimens combined with flucytosine or fluconazole, or after 4–6 weeks of high-dose oral fluconazole induction and consolidation therapy. 23. Discontinuation of antifungal maintenance treatment in successfully treated HIV-infected adults and adolescents with cryptococcal disease is recommended if they are stable, adherent to ART and antifungal therapy for at least one year, and meet specific criteria, such as a CD4 count ≥100 cells/mm³ and suppressed viral load. 24. For children aged 2–5 years with successfully treated cryptococcal disease, antifungal maintenance therapy can be discontinued if they are stable, adherent to ART and antifungal therapy for at least one year, and have a CD4 cell count percentage >25% or an absolute count above the threshold.
